n101.text: Last time, the CECL Genie showed us the four parts of a full answer: Choice, Evidence, Concept and Link.

n201b.text: Homework time! The Genie is ready.

n202.text: A little ant is hiding in this video. Can you spot it?

n204.text: Lock in first with your fingers. One finger for every point.

n302b.text: Choice: only when you must pick.

n303b.text: The Link: answer what was asked.

n401.text: Question one. Ali wants to find out if more batteries make an electromagnet stronger. Set-up A has an iron nail, ten turns of wire and one battery. Set-up B has a steel nail, twenty turns of wire and two batteries. Explain why Ali's experiment is not a fair test.

n402.text: Round one. Does this answer need a Choice? One, yes. Two, no. Show me your fingers.

n404p.text: One. Every answer starts with a Choice!

n405b.text: Two! The question says explain. There is nothing to pick.

n406m.text: Two. A Choice is only for questions like which, or do you agree.

n501.text: The answer is two! Did you show two fingers? Put one finger up!

n502b.text: A choice is the answer you pick when the question asks you to pick, such as: yes, I agree, or bar X!

n602.text: Look closer. Start with the Evidence. What did Ali change? Your turn.

n603.text: Ali changed the type of nail, the number of turns of wire, and the number of batteries.

n604.text: Now the Concept, the rule for a fair test.

n605.text: In a fair test, only one variable is changed. The other variables are kept the same.

n607.text: Thus, Ali cannot be sure that the number of batteries made the electromagnet stronger.

n609.text: Give a Choice only when the question asks you to pick.

n701.text: Question two. Siti says that a cockroach has the same life cycle as a butterfly. Do you agree? Explain.

n702.text: Showdown! Double points. Basil's answer is missing one part. Is it one, the Choice, two, the Evidence, three, the Concept, or four, the Link?

n704m.text: Four! Basil never says what the question asked: is it the same life cycle?

n705.text: Thus, the cockroach and the butterfly do not have the same life cycle.

n706.text: Four fingers? Put up two more on your score hand!

n801.text: Be the Link! Shrink down. Quietly.

n802.text: You are a short green sentence. On one side, the science rule. On the other side, the question.

n803.text: You stretch out, and join them together. Thus, the cockroach and the butterfly do not have the same life cycle.

n901p.text: Here is my answer to the fridge question. Magnets attract steel.

n902.text: Look closer. Explain why the door of a refrigerator stays closed. Pip wrote a true Concept. But it is only one part. Your turn: what does the question show? And what does it ask?

n903.text: Evidence: there is a strip of magnet inside the edge of the door, and the body of the refrigerator is made of steel.

n904.text: Link: Thus, the magnetic strip is attracted to the steel body, and this keeps the door closed.

n905m.text: A link is the sentence that joins the science rule to what the question asks, such as: thus, this keeps the door closed!

n906.text: If you help with one thing, help with the Link.

n908.text: The Link joins the rule to what the question asks. It often starts with Thus.

n1101.text: Show me your score hand! Two fingers or more? You beat the Buddies. Three fingers? High five!

n1102.text: Did you spot the ant? It was on the window ledge!

n1103p.text: Here is a fun fact! An ant leaves a smell trail from the food to its nest, and the other ants follow it. It is a link!

n1201.text: You can learn the CECL way with the Genie in TheOneApp. Open TheOneApp, tap Questions, then the CECL Genie. The Genie is for members.

n1202b.text: CECL means Choice, Evidence, Concept and Link, such as Momo's full answer about bar X!
